title: Sentence Reordering
description: Master sentence reordering for Grade 9: rearranging jumbled words into sentences and jumbled sentences into a coherent paragraph, with clear strategies — bilingual notes, practice and tests.

topics.title: Reordering Jumbled Words
topics.concept:
To rebuild a sentence from jumbled words:

  1. Find the subject (who/what the sentence is about) and the main verb.
  2. Attach the object that completes the verb.
  3. Slot in modifiers in the order manner → place → time.
  4. Check the articles, prepositions and capital letter.

For questions, the order changes: question word + auxiliary + subject + verb. Where / are / you / going → Where are you going?

Watch the natural adjective order (a small red wooden box) and keep the verb agreeing with its subject.

examples.solution: She read the book quietly. — S + V + O + manner.

examples.problem: Reorder into a question: going / you / where / are
examples.solution: Where are you going? — wh-word + auxiliary + subject + verb.

recap: Order: Subject + Verb + Object + manner + place + time
Check articles, prepositions, adjective order and capital letter

topics.title: Reordering Jumbled Sentences into a Paragraph
topics.concept:
When whole sentences are jumbled, arrange them into a logical paragraph:

  1. Find the opening sentence — it introduces the topic and has no pronoun referring to an earlier idea.
  2. Follow the pronouns — 'he', 'it', 'they', 'this' must refer to a noun already mentioned, so they come after that noun.
  3. Use connectors — 'however', 'therefore', 'finally', 'as a result' link to a previous idea, so they signal a later position.
  4. Follow time and cause-effect order — earlier events and causes come first.
  5. Find the closing sentence — it concludes, summarises, or states a result.

examples.problem:
Which is the opening sentence?
(a) However, it was too late.
(b) A fire broke out in the factory.
examples.solution: (b) — it introduces the topic; (a) begins with 'However', so it must follow another idea.

examples.problem: Order: (1) She studied hard. (2) Riya had an exam. (3) She passed with distinction.
examples.solution: 2 → 1 → 3 — introduce Riya, then the cause (studied), then the result (passed).

recap: Opening sentence introduces the topic (no back-referring pronoun)
Pronouns and connectors point backward → they come later
Follow time and cause-effect; the closing sentence concludes

questions.q: Reorder: 'the / opened / she / door'
Reorder: 'going / are / where / they'
Which opens a paragraph?
options: A new shop opened in town.

questions.q: Reorder: 'hard / studied / he / for / exam / the'
options: He studied hard for the exam.
He hard studied for the exam.
For the exam he hard studied.
Studied he hard for the exam.

questions.q: Correct order: 'a / box / small / red'
A sentence with 'Finally' usually appears:
Reorder: 'I / a / read / book / yesterday'
Order: (1) It started to bark. (2) A dog saw a stranger. (3) The stranger ran away.
Reorder the question: 'did / what / say / he'
Which cannot be the opening sentence?
questions.explanation: 'But' links back, so it can't open.

questions.q: Reorder: 'every / temple / he / visits / the / morning'
options: He visits the temple every morning.
Every morning the temple he visits.
He the temple visits every morning.
Visits he the temple every morning.

questions.q: A back-referring pronoun ('it', 'they') in a sentence means it:
options: follows the noun it refers to
questions.explanation: Pronouns must follow the noun they refer to.

questions.q: Reorder: 'so / tired / was / he / that / asleep / fell / he'
options: He was so tired that he fell asleep.
He so tired was that he fell asleep.
So tired he was that fell asleep he.
He fell asleep so tired that he was.
questions.explanation: 'so … that …' result structure with correct S-V order.

questions.q: Order: (P) Soon, dark clouds gathered. (Q) The travellers set out at dawn. (R) They hurried to find shelter. (S) Within an hour, it began to rain.
questions.explanation: Set out → clouds gather → rain → hurry for shelter (time order).

questions.q: Reorder: 'never / such / I / a / have / seen / sight'
options: I have never seen such a sight.
Never I have seen such a sight.
Such a sight I have never seen.
I never have seen such a sight.

questions.q: Which sentence is the closer? (a) Hard work, therefore, always pays. (b) Many students doubted him. (c) Ravi practised for hours daily. (d) Eventually, he won the championship.
questions.explanation: A general concluding statement with 'therefore' rounds off the paragraph.

questions.q: Reorder (formal inversion): 'had / hardly / sat / I / down / when / rang / the / bell'
options: Hardly had I sat down when the bell rang.
I hardly had sat down when the bell rang.
Hardly I had sat down when the bell rang.
Had hardly I sat down the bell rang when.
questions.explanation: Negative-adverb inversion: 'Hardly had I sat down when …'.

questions.q: Order: (1) This habit improved his health. (2) Arjun decided to wake up early. (3) He started jogging every day.
Reorder: 'the / which / book / I / bought / interesting / was'
options: The book which I bought was interesting.
The book was which I bought interesting.
Which I bought the book was interesting.
Interesting was the book which I bought.

questions.q: Which is the most logical opening? (about a discovery)
options: As a result, the world changed.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming made a surprising discovery.
questions.explanation: It introduces the topic with a clear subject and time, no back-reference.

intro.en: English follows a fairly strict word order: usually Subject–Verb–Object, with describing words and time/place phrases in predictable spots. Reordering tasks scramble words or whole sentences and ask you to restore that order. The trick is to find the anchor — the subject and verb — and build outward.
intro.hi: अंग्रेज़ी का शब्द-क्रम काफी निश्चित है: प्रायः Subject–Verb–Object, और विशेषण व समय/स्थान-वाक्यांश तय स्थानों पर। Reordering प्रश्न शब्दों या पूरे वाक्यों को उलट देते हैं और सही क्रम बहाल करने को कहते हैं। तरकीब है — आधार खोजें — कर्ता और क्रिया — और बाहर की ओर बनाते जाएँ।

real_life.situation:
A jumbled note from a friend:

Jumbled: party / the / at / meet / us / six / will / she

Ordered: She will meet us at the party at six.
real_life.why: Find the subject (She), then the verb (will meet), then the object (us), then the place/time phrases. Word order is logical, not random — and reordering simply rebuilds that logic.

quick_test.q: A sentence beginning with 'However' in a jumbled set is usually:
quick_test.explanation: 'However' links back to a previous idea, so it cannot open the paragraph.

common_mistakes.right: Start with the topic sentence; 'Therefore' comes later.
common_mistakes.note: Connectors of result point back to a cause.

reading.passage:
Order these four sentences into a paragraph:

(P) The villagers thanked the young boy.
(Q) One evening, a flood swept through the village.
(R) A brave boy warned everyone in time.
(S) Because of his warning, all the families escaped safely.

Correct order: Q → R → S → P.

questions.q: Which sentence opens the paragraph and why?
questions.answer: Q — it introduces the event (the flood) with no back-referring pronoun.

questions.q: Why does S come before P?
questions.answer: S explains the result of the warning; P (thanking) is the natural conclusion that follows.

questions.q: What clue tells you P is the closing sentence?
questions.answer: It expresses gratitude/conclusion and refers back to 'the young boy' already introduced.

speaking: She goes to school every morning.
Where are you going so early?
They played football in the park yesterday.
First we planned, then we acted.
Finally, the team lifted the trophy.

writing.prompt: Write four short sentences that tell a tiny story, then jumble their order and give the correct sequence as an answer — like a reordering question.
writing.example: Jumbled: (1) He apologised. (2) Sam broke the vase. (3) His mother forgave him. Answer: 2 → 1 → 3.

micro_quiz.explanation: S + V + manner: 'He runs very fast.'

micro_quiz.q: Reorder the question: 'are / where / you / from'

micro_quiz.explanation: The topic sentence opens; connectors and back-referring pronouns come later.
'Therefore' shows a result, so it follows a cause.

challenge.q: Order: (1) It grew into a tall tree. (2) A boy planted a seed. (3) Years later, it gave cool shade.
challenge.explanation: Plant the seed → it grows → it gives shade (time/cause order).

challenge.q: Reorder: 'so / it / late / we / was / left'
options: It was so late we left.
It was late, so we left.
So late it was we left.
We left it was so late.
challenge.explanation: 'It was late, so we left.' is the natural cause-result order.

challenge.q: Which sentence must come last? (a) The crowd cheered wildly. (b) The striker scored the winning goal. (c) The whistle blew for the match to start.
challenge.explanation: Start → goal → cheering: (a) is the concluding reaction.
